To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the emergence of stimulus equivalence classes can be followed by a reversal of baseline relations, and that this reversal does not necessarily disrupt the transitivity and equivalence relations that had been previously established.
baseline and symmetry versus equivalence relations were not affected in the same way by the same manipulations.
baseline relations are not always reversed when a baseline conditional discrimination is reversed, and the reversal of baseline relations may not be necessary for stimulus equivalence to occur.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how the baseline relations established between stimuli affect subsequent equivalence class formation and the emergence of transitive relations between stimuli that are not directly trained.
the development and evaluation of an experimental model of stimulus control and equivalence that is sensitive to changes in the environment and the effects of these changes.
the question of whether the emergence of equivalence classes is an automatic byproduct of stimulus pairing or whether it reflects a more complex process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
equivalence relations are extremely robust and are not easily disrupted, whereas baseline relations are highly sensitive and are readily modified.
the baseline and symmetry relations are not equivalent to transitivity/equivalance relations, and that the latter are not equivalent to baseline and symmetry relations.
baseline relations are not necessarily equivalent to symmetry relations and that the two sets of relations are not always interchangeable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the baseline conditional discrimination training and reversal phases were sufficient for producing stimulus control over responding in the equivalence classes, but that these classes were not necessarily sufficient for producing control over responding in baseline and symmetry probes.
the emergence of equivalence classes can be extremely robust and resistant to subsequent modifications, but the baseline conditional relations can also be extremely robust and sensitive to changes.

equivalence classes are not rigid structures that are resistant to changes in baseline contingencies, but instead are flexible and dynamic structures that are sensitive to the reinforcement history of the baseline conditional discrimination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
equivalence classes may not be as stable as they are typically portrayed to be in the literature.
the baseline relations that emerge during the establishment of equivalence classes can be modified in a variety of ways.
the baseline conditional discriminations are critical in determining the patterns of symmetry and transitivity/equivalences.
